meta.description: Genuine Jim Collins: the opening line of Good to Great (2001). It flips the older proverb 'the best is the enemy of the good' that Voltaire quoted in 1770.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Good is the enemy of great'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Jim Collins opens Good to Great (2001) with it. It inverts the old saying Voltaire quoted, 'the best is the enemy of the good.'

Chapter 1, “Good Is the Enemy of Great” — opening sentence

source.excerpt: Good is the enemy of great. And that is one of the key reasons why we have so little that becomes great. We don’t have great schools, principally because we have good schools. We don’t have great government, principally because we have good government. Few people attain great lives, in large part because it is just so easy to settle for a good life.
trail: A November 2001 review in The Nation, “Jack Welch, Move Over,” reports that “In Good to Great, he argues that ‘good is the enemy of great.’” The Nation ↗
The Objective Standard’s review opens: “‘Good is the enemy of great,’ writes Jim Collins in the opening line of Good to Great” (New York: HarperCollins, 2001). The Objective Standard ↗
Collins’s official website has an audio piece titled “Good is the Enemy of Great,” in which he restates the idea in his own voice. jimcollins.com ↗

Wikiquote’s Jim Collins page lists the line under his 2005 monograph Good to Great and the Social Sectors: “Good is the enemy of great. That good is the enemy of great is not just a business problem. It is a human problem.” Wikiquote ↗

author.bio: James C. “Jim” Collins is an American researcher, author and speaker on business management. He began his research and teaching career on the faculty of Stanford’s Graduate School of Business in 1988. He co-wrote Built to Last (1994) with Jerry I. Porras, then wrote Good to Great (2001) on his own; it opens with this line.

misattribution.heading: Often confused with an older proverb
misattribution.intro: Collins’s line is genuine. People often mix it up with a much older saying that runs the other way: the old proverb warns that chasing the best spoils the good, while Collins warns that settling for good blocks the great.

items.why: In 1770 Voltaire quoted an Italian proverb, “Il meglio è l’inimico del bene” (“the best is the enemy of the good”), and later used “le mieux est l’ennemi du bien” in his poem La Bégueule. That is the opposite warning, not Collins’s line. Wikipedia ↗

Around 1726 Montesquieu wrote in his Pensées, “Le mieux est le mortel ennemi du bien” (“the best is the mortal enemy of the good”). This is another form of the older idea, now often given as “Perfect is the enemy of good.” Wikipedia ↗

misattribution.truthLine: “Good is the enemy of great” itself is Jim Collins’s wording: it is the opening sentence of Good to Great (2001), as contemporary reviews confirm ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Collins used the line to open Good to Great and to set its thesis: organizations and people stay merely good because good is comfortable enough to remove the pressure to change. In the sentences right after it, he applies the idea to schools, government and individual lives, not only to companies.

The line became the book’s shorthand. A 2001 review in The Nation ↗ summarized his argument with it. Collins returned to it in his 2005 monograph Good to Great and the Social Sectors, as Wikiquote records ↗, where he called it “not just a business problem” but “a human problem.”
context.pull: Few people attain great lives, in large part because it is just so easy to settle for a good life.
